PS! U PERSONALITy OF THE MONTH
Alfred E. Driscoll, Delta Delta
By O. D. Keep,
ALFRED EASTLACK DRISCOLL,
/\ Delta Delta '25, is, at 43, one of the
youngest men ever elected Governor of
New Jersey and�of vastly more
importance
to its citizens�one of the ablest and most
high minded public figures to emerge in
that state in many years.
Ever since his graduation from Williams
College in 1925 and from the Harvard
in his undergraduate days) has been an
active participant in the long struggle to
free New Jersey from the control of the
Frank Hague political dictatorship, which
has operated not only through the Demo
cratic machine but also through the con
nivance of leading Republicans. Demo
cratic Governor Charles Edison and Re
publican Governor Walter E. Edge, during
the past six years, have trimmed Hague's
wings but it now remains for Brother Dris
coll to give the coup de grace to the un
holy political alliances that have long stood
in the way of .good government in the
state.
Few of his old friends or more recent
political allies doubt that he will accom
plish just that.
As the Newark Star-Ledger states: "At
43, Driscoll has been a first-rate law stu
dent, a successful lawyer and business
man, a successful political crusader in
Camden County against an intrenched and
corrupt political machine, a constructive
State Senator and a
remarkably successful
administrator as commissioner of the vital
and extremely complex Department of Al
coholic Beverage Control."
It should be added that Brother Driscoll
has acquired in his brief career a
charming
wife, the former Antoinette Ware Tatem,
like himself brought up in the pleasant old
town of Haddonfield in Camden County, a
twelve year old daughter and two sons,
nine and six respectively; the headship of
a
distinguished old Camden law firm; and
a statewide reputation for intelhgent and
reasonable pohtical uprightness that per-
'25, Governor of New Jersey
Delta Delta "25
mitted him to defeat for the Republican
Gubernatorial nomination last spring for
mer Governor Harold Hoffman, a
notably
effective vote-getter, and then to go on to
a
more-than-quarter-million-vote triumph
over the hand-picked Democratic candi
date of Boss Hague, who spent vast sums
and employed every unsavory pohtical
trick, of which he is the past grand master,
to defeat a man whose elevation to the
Governorship inevitably means a
sharp
curtailment of his power.
In his college days Brother DriscoU's
secret weapons of sti-ict integrity and warm
humanity made him a
popular figure on
the campus and at the Delta Delta and
more recently have won him the confidence
and affection of hundreds of thousands of
New Jersey voters.
Brother DriscoU has accomplished one
of the rarest things in pubhc life by main
taining completely his own
independence
and at the same time handling the "practi
cal" politicians so
disarmingly that even
the worst of them have found it difficult
to dislike him. Time and again as a State
Senator he was offered a
participation in
the "honest graft" which is the- common
place of state politics and which takes so
many agreeable forms. His associates were
constantly amazed at his statement that he
never mixed his politics with his law prac
tice or business interests.
One of his closest political friends told
this vsTiter he had suggested to Driscoll,
when, as Alcohol Beverage Commissioner,
he was
virtually the czar of the New Jersey
liquor industry, that he should use his
position to build a
personal political ma
chine which might come ui handy at some
future date. Certainly nine men out of ten
would have seen little impropriety in such
a
policy, but Driscoll was the tenth man
and smilingly rejected the suggestion-to
the amazement and admiration of his in
fluential friend who later materially aided
in getting him the designation as the candi
date of the state organization.

In the late Twenties and in the Thirties,
when New Jersey groaned under state
government as bad as that of almost any
state in the Union, Driscoll worked val
iantly and without thought of consequences
for every cause of good government that
came
along and, at least in state matters,
found himself almost invariably on the
losing team. The writer knows from inti
mate association how many thousands of
hours the new Governor gave during his
early days as a
young lawyer to one un
successful campaign after another designed
to elect nien pledged to rid New Jersey of
Hagueism.
Unlike most men Driscoll thrived on
political adversity and acquired the experi
ence and the following which has since
served him well. He became a member of
the Haddonfield Board of Education, being
President in 1937, when he was also
elected Haddonfield Borough Commission
er and chosen Director of Revenue and Fi
nance. He reduced his community's debt
by 47% and its local tax rate by 22%. In
1938 he became State Senator and, two
years later. Senate Majority Leader.. In
1941 he was
unanimously elected by the
State Legislature, Commissioner of Alco
holic Beverage Control, where his admin
istration won nation-wide acclaim and
praise from such dissimilar groups as the
W.C.T.U. and the Retail Beverage Associ
ation.
In this extremely difficult job Driscoll
demonstrated again his unusual capacity
for scrupulous fairness, sweet reasonable
ness, and effective administration, and in
so doing became automatically available
for the Governorship when a
plethora of
eager aspirants compelled the party's lead
ers to designate a candidate acceptable to
most of the contending factions.
Politics in New Jersey is no child's play
and two more formidable opponents than
former Governor Hoffman and Frank
Hague would be difficult to find in one
hfe time, but the cold fact is that Driscoll
has whipped them both and enhanced his
reputation as an honorable and reasonable
man in the process. Noble-minded re
formers are the summer soldiers of politics;
few endure. They either become cynical
and sell out in one
way or another to be
elected, or
they never learn how to imple
ment their idealism and so lose to lesser
but shi-ewder men. Brother Driscoll was
notable as an
undergraduate as a man of
high purpose and inflexible integrity who
at the same time was no
prig about it and
was able to see the good qualities and
even
enjoy the society of men of lesser
worth. It is these qualities which have
made Driscoll personally popular as well
as widely respected; they are also the
qualities that will in all probability make
him an effective Governor, cap.able of
bringing about the reforms for which en
lightened people in New Jersey have long
been clamoring.
Already there are those who look for
ward to seeing Brother Driscoll in the
United States Senate where his keen in
telligence and capacity for study and
analysis would give an even wider field
foi his talents. Meanwhile, the new Gov
ernor of New Jersey is intent only on the
job at hand�and on
getting back a few of
the pounds he lost in his recent struggles
with Messers. Hoffman and Hague.
Leaner today by ten pounds than when
he ran some of the fastest half miles ever
seen in Williamstown and starred at winter
sports, Driscoll is as hard as nails physi
cally and not much older looking than
twenty years ago. His life has been a full
one and he has had little time for diver
sions outside his family life. But for years
he used to return to Williamstown with old
friends to ski on the slopes of Greylock and
the Dome and it is as like as not that he
will resume the custom once he has New
Jersey under control. His many friends of
the Delta Delta, many of whom return to
Williamstown each winter, will be looking
for the Governor when the snow flies next
year in Western Massachusetts.

ANNALS COMMITTEE
ALBERT
C. JACOBS, Phi, '21, former
i Editor of The Diamond, and Peter

ner for the members of the Committee on
The Annals of Psi Upsilon in honor of
Earl D. Babst, Iota '93, Chairman of The
Annals Committee and former President of
the Executive Council of Psi Upsilon. The
Earl D. Babst, lota '93
dinner was held in the Board of Governors
Room at the Columbia University Club on
Sunday, November 24.
Those present were Brother Babst,
Brother Henry N. Woolman, Tau '96,
Brother Edward L. Stevens, Chi '99,
Brother Walter T. Collins, Iota '03,
Brother Jacobs and Brother GaBauer. Be
fore the dinner the guests sang The Dox
ology and stood in silence for a moment
in memory of the late and dearly beloved
Brother Archibald Douglas, Lambda '94,
onetime President of the Executive Coun
cil, and the only member of The Annals
Committee not present at the dinner.
After dinner a recorded statement in
honor of Brother Babst was made, having
been prepared and recorded by Brother
Jacobs, and an illuminated scroll contain
ing the same material and signed by all
the living members of the Committee was
presented to him. The text of this follows;
TO
BROTHER EARL D. BABST,
IOTA-PHI '93
Exactly one hundred and thirteen years
ago our venerable Fraternity was founded
at old Union. And just five years have
passed since the publication of The Annals
of Psi Upsilon. On this memorable day,
November 24, 1946, we, who were
privi
leged to serve with you as members of
The Annals' Committee, have assembled
at the Columbia University Club in New
York City to pay tribute from the heart to
you and to your nearly six decades of
devotion to Psi Upsilon. You have called
it a "labor of love," but a
"happy labor."
Since that day in the autumn of 1889,
when at the Hall of the Iota you heard for
the first time "that mysterious combination
of Greek Letters" we all love so well, you
have been a
pillar of our Fraternity, wise
and understanding in its councils, inter
preting its wonderful romance, its mystic
symbols and its priceless heritage of broth
erly love to thousands of Psi U's.
A guardian of the highest ideals and tra
ditions of the American college fraternity,
you have combined to a rare
degree that
ardent love and faithful service to Alma
Mater, which in your case has included
both Kenyon and Michigan from which
institutions you hold degrees honoris causa,
with undying devotion and endless loyalty
to Psi Upsilon. You have fully appreciated
the great part that fraternities have played
in the buflding and development of our
colleges and universities of today. Your
magnificent service to Kenyon and Michi
gan has been enriched by your associations
in Psi Upsilon. You have never
forgotten
tliat the fraternity is but a
part of Alma

Mater; and, as a member of Phi Beta
Kappa, have sought to maintain the tra
ditions of scholarship on which our
Society
was founded.
We hail you for collecting and preserv
ing for posterity the records and the
memorabilia of our
Fraternity. Inspired, as
you were, during your formative years, by
close association with one of our
greatest
historians, by his mastery of detail, by his
painstaking research, and by his knowledge
of fraternity heraldry, you early began to
record in romantic and telling phrases the
heritage of Psi Upsilon. The spark then
kindled has never dimmed, but has burned
brighter through the years. Due to your
tireless interest, your diligent efforts, and
your exacting love of detail, Psi U. has be
come the custodian of the foremost collec
tion of college and fraternity lore. Our
Archives are a
lasting monument to your in
dustry and foresight. Your love of Psi
Upsilon, your never-to-be-forgotten experi
ences with the brothers of "the then and
now," and your beautiful recording of
those marvelous days of yore�are forever
preserved for future generations in that
delightful book, "Occasions In Psi Upsi
lon," which contains your many graceful
and learned addresses at Fraternity gather
ings. And from you the Diamond of Psi
Upsilon has always received generous and
valuable support.
After treading our ancient halls for over
half a
century, your long cherished plans
for a definitive history of our Fraternity
culminated at last in The Annals. Without
your magnetic inspiration, your wise
leadership and your unselfish cooperation,
this monumental work, unique in the fra
ternity world, would never have been
forthcoming, and the heritage of Taylor,
Fiske and Jacobs would not have been
readily available to the Psi U's of today.
In The Annals you were the gifted
chronicler of more than a
century of our
Conventions, with which you became ex
perienced at an
early date, for as
delegate
of the Phi you carried to the 1893 Con
vention at the Zeta the petition which three
years later gave birth to the Rho Chapter.
On this, the fifth Anniversary of The
Annals, we
glory in its exalted position
among fraternity histories, in the splendid
way it has brought the real meaning of the
college fraternity to our
campuses of today.
As chairman of the Committee you must
be rightly proud of its unparalleled success.
One of our
country's leading citizens and
an international figure in the business
world, you have never lost touch with the
spirit of Alma Mater and Psi Upsilon.
Whether in Crestline, Ohio, or at 120 Wall
Street, that spirit has been nurtured and
has matured. A generous benefactor of
Kenyon and the Iota, of the hallowed
"Dear Old Spot" to vvhich you have always
referred with such loving tenderness, of
Michigan and the Phi, and of the Frater
nity, you have found time to serve in your
human, understanding and discreet way
both college and Psi Upsilon. At one time
a valued and honored trustee of Kenyon,
formerly President of the Kenyon Alumni
Association of the East, always active in
the affairs of Michigan and in its alumni
activities, a former President of the Uni
versity of Michigan Club of New York,
presently editor and historian of essays
about that remarkable group of Michigan
men who were so
prominent in the Cleve
land administration, you were also a dis
tinguished member of our Executive Coun
cil from 1908 to 1928. We were fortunate
indeed to have you as its wise and lovable
President, our
highest office of trust and
honor, from 1924 to 1928, a most im
portant period, following as it did the long
tenure of Brother Herbert L. -Bridgman,
Gamma '66. Under your leadership as the
sixth President of our Council, we recall
the fitting installation of our second
Canadian Chapter, the Epsilon Phi, at
McGill University on March 17, 1928, one
of the eleven jewels added to the crown
of Psi Upsilon since you graced our ranks.
Resigning as President of the Council
in 1928 because of your democratic under
standing of the office you so
ably held,
though Psi U's everywhere urged you to

outstanding service to the Fraternity has
gone on unabated. And through the many

Summary of What Trar
Meeting of September 9, 1946
The Executive Council met in New York
on
September 9, 1946. President Scott
Turner presided.
The Treasurer presented a written re
port of the status of the investments. He
also reported that dues had been paid, for
the current year by all undergraduate
Chapters and that there were no accounts
receivable. The report was
approved.
The President exhibited a
report of
scholastic averages at the University of
California, showing the Epsilon's standing
as sixth out of 20 men's groups on the
campus.
The President read a letter from Brother
Harold L. Berry, Kappa '01, dated Sep
tember 11, 1946, submitting his resignation
from the Executive Council. It was voted
that Brother Berry's resignation be ac
cepted with regret and with appreciation
for his years of service. After discussion it
was voted that Robert S. Taylor, Jr., Eta
'25, be elected to the Executive Council to
fill Brother Berry's term, which expires
with the Convention of 1949.
The President read a letter from the
President of the Delta Delta Alumni As
sociation, notifying the Councfl of the re
sumption of undergraduate Chapter ac
tivities at Wflliams, with 13 Brothers and
eight pledges. It was
